t: Smallest Substring With Identical Characters I — Binary Search on the Answer
o: We may flip up to `numOps` characters of a binary string and want to minimize the length of the longest run of identical characters. The key observation is monotonicity: if every run can be shortened to length `m`, it can certainly be shortened to length `m+1`, so feasibility is monotone in `m` and we can binary search the answer. A run of length `L` needs exactly `floor(L / (m+1))` flips to be broken into pieces of length at most `m` (each flip splits off one chunk of size `m+1`). For example, in "000001" with 1 op, `m=2` works (run of 5 needs one flip), while `m=1` would need 3 flips, so the answer is 2. With `n ≤ 1000`, even an O(n²) enumeration of candidate answers is affordable.
k: Feasibility of an answer `m` is monotone, enabling binary search.
A run of length L costs floor(L/(m+1)) flips to cap all its pieces at m.
Only maximal runs of identical characters matter; flips inside them are independent.

a.i: Binary search the smallest `m` such that the total flips needed to cap every maximal run at length `m` is at most `numOps`. The check scans the string once, summing `runLength // (m+1)` over runs.
s: Define check(m): scan maximal runs, sum floor(len/(m+1)), return whether the sum ≤ numOps.
Binary search m in [1, n] for the smallest feasible value.
a.t: O(n log n) — each feasibility check is O(n) and binary search does O(log n) checks.

a.i: Since n ≤ 1000, we can simply try m = 1, 2, …, n and return the first feasible value using the same run-cost check. This avoids binary search reasoning and is trivially correct because feasibility is monotone.
s: For m from 1 to n, compute the total flip cost over all runs.
Return the first m whose cost is ≤ numOps.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — up to n candidate answers, each checked in O(n); fine for n ≤ 1000.

w: Use the binary-search version in an interview — it generalizes to the hard version with n up to 5·10⁵. Pitfalls: forgetting that a run of length L needs floor(L/(m+1)) flips (not ceil(L/m), though they coincide here), and answering 0 — the answer is at least 1 since any single character is itself a run. Follow-ups: the hard version (n up to 5·10⁵) needs exactly this binary search; another variant asks for the minimum number of ops for a target length, which is the same check.
